newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco talks could fold on liability issues.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco talks could fold on liability issues.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent
Tobacco settlement negotiators are making a last-ditch effort to reach a deal this week, but several sources close to the talks warned Monday their efforts could unravel in the next few days.

A large meeting of attorneys general, the highest ranking legal officers in each state, that had been scheduled for Tuesday in Dallas has been cancelled, and instead core negotiators are now in Washington.
They are still struggling to solve several critical civil liability problems that may prove to be unsurmountable.

At issue is whether the parties can devise a plan that would give cigarette companies some certainty about damages they would have to pay without depriving individuals of their right to sue the tobacco industry.

Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore, a lead negotiator for the states, said one of the disputed areas involves punitive damages, which are awarded to punish or deter certain behaviour or activities.
He said his colleagues have refused to agree to a proposal that would deny individuals a right to pursue such damages.
"We told them we won't give it up, and they say they want it," he said in a telephone interview late Sunday night.
A source close to the talks said Monday the attorneys general also do not want to give in to the tobacco industry's demand that it be protected from class-action lawsuits.
He also said the industry wants immunity from certain secondhand smoke lawsuits.
The source said he was not optimistic these issues could be resolved any time soon and that the talks could disband by midweek.
Moore said that while talks were "tough" at this point, progress was being made and that he remained hopeful a deal could be reached. "I think we'll get there," he said.
He said the industry has agreed to some health care concessions that could not have be achieved without a settlement.
"There's nothing else that could accomplish these gains," he said.
Powerful health groups have raised objections to a quick deal and formed a coalition that met last week to try to ensure that health issues are addressed in any agreement.

The American Cancer Society said Monday it now believes that certain concepts to be included in a proposed settlement address its public health concerns, including efforts to stop smoking among children.

"We are encouraged by the proposals we have heard so far and we urge the attorneys general to bring forward a complete plan so that a full public health evaluation can be conducted," American Cancer Society Chairman George Dessart said in a statement.

The group said a settlement that helps produce a smoke-free generation as soon as possible would be better in controlling cancer than waiting for the "uncertain result of many years of continued litigation."

Sources said that under a current proposal the tobacco industry would be subject to steep financial penalities if underage smoking is not reduced 30 percent in five years and 60 percent in 10 years. It would also agree to new advertising restrictions, warning labels and certain federal Food and Drug Administration control.

There are now at least 34 states that have sued the tobacco industry to recoup Medicaid health care costs of smokers. The top legal officers of some of those states, along with plaintiffs lawyers handling class action cases and members of the health community began negotiating with the industry in early April.

Last week, James Tierney, who is helping coordinate the states' legal efforts, said he believed the parties were "heading towards a settlement" but warned it could take "a couple of trials" to make both sides willing to reach a deal.

Moore has been trying to reach a deal ahead of the July 7 trial date in his state's case against the industry. The Mississippi case is scheduled to be the first of the state Medicaid suits to go to trial, followed by Florida and Texas.
Both the White House and key members of Congress, who would most likely have to approve any settlement, indicated last week they would not agree to any hastily reached accord.
